title: Agent-like URLQuery reports cluster in ten weeks of spring 2026, half of them at UNCTAD, and most rest only on a web address match

sentences.text: URLQuery is a public service that loads a submitted web address in a sandboxed browser and records the requests the page makes ([RuntimeWire](https://runtimewire.com/article/openai-agents-unctad-stat-api-workarounds)) [[call:7e554e8e/33#L11]].
This package lists [[38,160|README.md#L7]] URLQuery reports.
Its builders count [[37,649|card:84aa5fe1@out0#L1]] of them as "included", meaning they look like automated agents fetching data from public sites, mostly statistics sites.

Of these, [[36,836|card:84aa5fe1@out0#L2]] date from April 13 to June 21, 2026, and [[19,319|card:84aa5fe1@out0#L5]], about half, concern UNCTAD, the statistics site of the United Nations trade and development body.
The evidence behind them is uneven.
[[26,533|card:b2835e4f@out0#L3]] cite nothing beyond a web address that matched a target site.

[[6,464|card:b2835e4f@out0#L4]] contain submitted code written to fetch data or post a form, the catalog's strongest evidence, and [[6,315|card:e2e3a3fc@out0#L1]] of these are also on an outside list whose selection rule the package does not give.
The recorded methods move from plain page requests to custom programs and, in June, what the reviewers call URLQuery account attempts.
But the first programs appear at the same moment as the outside list, so this change may show what was captured rather than how the activity changed.
No file says who ran any of it.

figures.caption: Included reports per week: almost all fall between mid-April and late June 2026, and UNCTAD is the largest source

sections.heading: Each row is one report with a time, a stated reason and the builders' judgment, but no report contents

sentences.text: Each row gives a report's link, its time in UTC to the second, a disposition, a method class and a reason built from fixed sentences [[all-reports.csv#row=18989]].
The package holds none of the report data itself: no report JSON, response bodies, submitted code or screenshots [[README.md#L3]].
The disposition is "included" for 37,649 reports, "background" for 79 kept as examples of ordinary traffic, and "review required" for 432 held without a judgment [[README.md#L8]].
Included reports are rated "significant" (6,467) or "suggestive" (31,182), a qualitative judgment and not a probability [[README.md#L8]] [[README.md#L41]].
In practice, all [[6,464|call:7e554e8e/39#L5]] reports with code are significant, and only [[3|call:7e554e8e/39#L5]] others are.
The reasons name three kinds of evidence, from weakest to strongest.
A web address in the report matches a target site's domain or a task identifier, an ID for one specific dataset or document.
The submission goes through an intermediary, such as a proxy, or itself publishes task data [[methods.json#/35]].
Or the submission contains code, decoded by the builders, written to fetch data or post a form [[methods.json#/34]].
Three UNCTAD reports filed within 26 seconds show how each kind adds to the one before.

history.text: The three UNCTAD reports below show one of each.

figures.caption: Three UNCTAD reports within 26 seconds: each adds evidence to the one before, and only the one with code is rated significant

sections.heading: The activity came in one burst, aimed at a few public data sites

sentences.text: Only [[756|call:7e554e8e/353#L9]] included reports come before April 13, 2026 and [[57|call:7e554e8e/353#L9]] after June 21.

After UNCTAD's trade statistics, the largest sources are Thrill Data's theme-park wait times, with [[5,100|card:84aa5fe1@out0#L6]] reports, and the Australian health statistics of AIHW, with [[4,844|card:84aa5fe1@out0#L7]] [[methods.json#/0]] [[methods.json#/4]].
Seven of the ten largest sources have their first included report in April to June 2026 [[card:67c6fe70@out0#L1]].

AIHW has [[4,837|card:67c6fe70#in%20largest%20burst/AIHW]] of its [[4,844|card:67c6fe70#reports/AIHW]] reports in one stretch with no gap of 6 hours or more, in the week of June 15 [[card:84aa5fe1#reports/63]].
Thrill Data is the main exception, with [[325|card:67c6fe70#before%20Apr%202026/Thrill%20Data]] reports before April.

sections.heading: Only about one included report in six contains code

sentences.text: A rule-based label added in this analysis, "evidence basis", sorts each included report by the strongest evidence its reason names [[concept:b436b78d]].

Of the [[37,649|card:b2835e4f@out0#L1]], [[26,533|card:b2835e4f@out0#L3]] cite only a web address match, [[4,480|card:b2835e4f@out0#L5]] an intermediary, [[6,464|card:b2835e4f@out0#L4]] code, and [[172|card:b2835e4f@out0#L6]] other evidence.
The figures say "task code or payload", since a few code reports are probe requests rather than programs.
The builders note that code shows intent, not that it ran [[methods.json#/34]].
The code is concentrated.

UNCTAD has [[4,853|card:b2835e4f#reports/26]] of the code reports, while six of the ten largest sources have five or fewer each: Woodlands House School, GBBC, MAX budget documents, Maryland school report cards, Drivelah and SEC county data [[call:7e554e8e/437#L5-L11]].
For these six, the files cannot rule out ordinary visits or security scans.
The builders keep examples of both as background controls, such as an "ordinary Thrill homepage visit" [[all-reports.csv#row=231]] and an "executable-path security scan" [[all-reports.csv#row=158]].
Five of the seven sources that start in April or later are among these six.
For UNCTAD, about half of the address-only reports fall close in time to code reports: [[7,004|call:7e554e8e/445#L1]] of [[13,673|card:b2835e4f#reports/25]] lie within five minutes of one.
When their times are moved one day later, only [[1,259|call:7e554e8e/445#L2]] do.
So these address matches come in the same bursts as the code, though timing alone does not show who submitted them.

figures.caption: Evidence basis by data source: code is concentrated in UNCTAD, Thrill Data, Mapillary and AIHW

sections.heading: Nearly all the code reports are also on one outside list

sentences.text: [[6,315|card:e2e3a3fc@out0#L1]] of the [[6,464|card:e2e3a3fc@out0#L1]] code reports carry a tag saying they are members of an "externally selected research-activity cohort".

The package defines this only as membership in a list kept by an outside website, a "research-activity explorer", as it stood on September 21, 2026, and gives no rule for how the list was chosen [[methods.json#/48]].
The tag marks membership, not the route by which a report entered the catalog.
Only [[337|card:e2e3a3fc@out0#L2]] of the [[26,533|card:e2e3a3fc@out0#L2]] address-only reports carry it.
The timing matches.
The first tagged report, at 19:46:36 UTC on March 6, 2026, comes six minutes before the first code report [[card:e2e3a3fc@out0#L3]] [[card:e2e3a3fc@out0#L4]].

All [[442|call:7e554e8e/371#L4]] included reports before 19:46 that day are plain requests, with no intermediary or code, and the first code report without the tag comes on April 18 [[card:e2e3a3fc@out0#L5]].
The files do not say why code and the tag go together.
The list may have been built by picking reports that contain code, or the builders may have looked for code mainly in reports on the list.
In the second case, code outside the list would be undercounted.

figures.caption: Included reports by evidence basis and membership in the outside list: 6,315 of 6,464 code reports are members, against 337 of 26,533 address-only reports

sections.heading: The recorded methods grew more elaborate, starting when the outside list starts

sentences.text: A sequence of dated events shows the change.
Some are episodes the builders reviewed by hand and named, and the others are bursts counted from the timestamps.
On November 12, 2025, Thrill Data gets [[44 source requests|card:0ee4c58f@out0#L2]].
The [[first custom programs|call:7e554e8e/371#L7]] come on March 6, 2026, aimed at the statistics of ONCB, the Thai drug-enforcement agency [[all-reports.csv#row=745]] [[methods.json#/2]].

On March 11 and 15, finished answer tables are encoded as Base64 text and submitted through httpbin.org, a public test service [[README.md#L34]], which the reviewers call [["Statistics deliberately embedded in scan pages"|all-reports.csv#row=773]].
Large bursts follow.
The busiest minute, at 17:06 UTC on April 29, holds [[63|call:7e554e8e/161#L1]] reports, all for UNCTAD [[card:0ee4c58f@out0#L7]].
On May 14 comes what the reviewers call "A complete UNCTAD archive split across 79 output URLs" [[all-reports.csv#row=13347]].
In June come programs the reviewers label "Disposable mailboxes used in URLQuery account attempts" [[all-reports.csv#row=29144]].
In September come programs whose decoded code holds "multi-endpoint Quidax API fetch probes" [[all-reports.csv#row=38085]].
Quidax is a Nigerian cryptocurrency exchange ([Guardian Nigeria](https://guardian.ng/technology/digital-assets-exchange-firm-quidax-launches-in-nigeria/)).

In June come programs the reviewers label [["Disposable mailboxes used in URLQuery account attempts"|all-reports.csv#row=29144]], and in September [[probe programs|all-reports.csv#row=38085]] for the transaction API of Quidax, a cryptocurrency exchange.

In June come programs the reviewers label [["Disposable mailboxes used in URLQuery account attempts"|all-reports.csv#row=29144]], and in September [[programs that probe several Quidax API endpoints|all-reports.csv#row=38085]].

Twelve dated events show the change.

sentences.text: The package holds none of the code behind these events [[README.md#L3]].
And because the first programs appear when the outside list begins, the timeline may show when the evidence gets stronger rather than when the activity changed.

sections.heading: The files do not show who ran the activity or how complete the catalog is

sentences.text: Every one of the [[38,160|call:7e554e8e/428#L84]] rows carries the same caveat: "Candidate evidence, not authenticated AI, OpenAI, RL-task or common-operator attribution." [[all-reports.csv#row=18989]]
That is, no row proves that an AI system, OpenAI, a reinforcement-learning training task or one common operator was behind it.

A news report quotes an independent researcher who considers similar UNCTAD records "highly likely" linked to OpenAI agents, and notes that the records do not name a model or show that one coordinated group made every request [[call:7e554e8e/48#L18]].
The builders link some tasks to a wiki or to paste sites, which are sites for sharing text publicly [[methods.json#/8]] [[methods.json#/21]].
The files do not say who posted them, so they do not settle whether one party ran everything.
The catalog is also not a census of URLQuery [[README.md#L22]] [[README.md#L43]].

Its [[41|card:a7856af1@out0#L9]] searches look for sites, documents and identifiers the builders already knew about [[methods.json#/8]] [[methods.json#/22]], so the files cannot show whether other sites saw a similar rise.

Some reports outside that focus appear anyway: [[183|call:7e554e8e/430#L3]] included reports are filed under "Source not identified", and hand-picked additions include sites that are not statistics sites, such as the disposable-mailbox service Boomlify, with [[22|call:7e554e8e/430#L3]] reports, and Quidax, with [[15|call:7e554e8e/430#L3]].

The searches also miss reports: the broadest UNCTAD search returned [[18,191|search-coverage.json#/32]], fewer than the [[19,300|call:7e554e8e/428#L4]] catalog reports matched to UNCTAD's address markers.
And [[300|call:7e554e8e/446#L8]] of the [[432|README.md#L8]] reports held for review predate April 2026, including [[109|call:7e554e8e/446#L4]] from November 13 to 15, 2023.
They name no data source, so the files do not record what they targeted.

[[114|card:ca822fc8#reports/Included%20only%20through%20an%20outside%20cohort%20tag]] included reports carry no evidence beyond the outside list's tag, and their reasons still begin with the "needs review" sentence of the reports held for review [[all-reports.csv#row=12868]].

[[124|card:ca822fc8#reports/Significant,%20but%20no%20data%20source%20named]] significant reports are filed under "Source not identified", so they are missing from every per-site count, and one of them is the reviewed UNCTAD archive above [[all-reports.csv#row=13347]].

And [[70|card:ca822fc8#reports/'Ordinary'%20MAX%20controls%20on%20May%2026%20(MAX%20burst%20day)]] of the [[73|card:ca822fc8#reports/'Ordinary'%20MAX%20controls,%20all%20dates]] controls labelled "Ordinary MAX portal/login traffic", for the US budget-document site max.gov [[methods.json#/5]], fall on May 26.
That is the day [[581|daily-source-counts.csv#row=195]] of the [[597|card:67c6fe70#reports/MAX%20budget%20documents]] MAX reports were filed, so some of these controls may belong to the same burst.
